title: Add Two Polynomials Represented as Linked Lists
statement:
A polynomial is stored as a singly linked list of `PolyNode` terms. Each node has an integer `coefficient`, a non-negative integer `power` (the term is `coefficient * x^power`) and `next`, the following term or `null`. Every list is in standard form: powers strictly decrease from head to tail and no term has coefficient `0`. The zero polynomial is the empty list, `null`.

Given the heads `poly1` and `poly2` of two such lists, return the head of a list in standard form for their sum (`null` when everything cancels). You may reuse the given nodes or make new ones with `new PolyNode(coefficient, power)`; an optional third argument sets `next`.

Each case is written as `[poly1, poly2]`, each polynomial listed as `[coefficient, power]` pairs from head to tail (`[]` for an empty list), and the answer is shown the same way. (The TypeScript starter types nodes as `_Node` because the signature format has no `PolyNode` type; the objects are `PolyNode`s.)
constraints: Each list has between 0 and 10^4 nodes
notes:
## Intuition

Adding polynomials means adding the coefficients of equal powers. Both lists are already sorted by power, highest first, so this is the merge step of merge sort: look at the two front terms, take the one with the higher power, and when the powers tie, combine them into one term. A simpler way is to total the coefficients per power in a hash map and rebuild a sorted list, but that needs a sort and extra memory; the merge does it in one pass.

## Approach

1. Make a `dummy` node so the result always has a node to append after; `tail` is its last node.
2. Walk `first` along `poly1` and `second` along `poly2` while both have terms.
3. If one front term has the higher power, link that node after `tail` and advance that list.
4. If the powers are equal, compute `sum`; append a new node only when `sum` is not 0, then advance both lists.
5. One list may still have terms, all with lower powers: link the rest of it after `tail`.
6. Return `dummy.next`, which is `null` when nothing survived.

## Example 1, step by step

`poly1` is `x` (`[1, 1]`) and `poly2` is `1` (`[1, 0]`). The front powers are 1 and 0, so `first` is linked after `dummy` and moves to `null`, which ends the loop. The leftover `second` is linked after it, giving `[[1, 1], [1, 0]]`, that is `x + 1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m + n): each step moves past at least one node.
- Space: O(1) besides the result, since existing nodes are reused and only combined terms are new.

## Pitfalls

- Equal powers whose coefficients cancel must produce no node at all; a `[0, p]` term breaks standard form.
- On equal powers advance both lists, or the same term is counted twice.
- Lists run from high power to low, so the larger power goes first, the opposite of merging ascending lists.
- Do not forget the leftover terms of the list that did not run out.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dummy` | placeholder before the result's first node |
| `tail` | last node of the result so far |
| `first`, `second` | current terms of `poly1` and `poly2` |
| `sum` | combined coefficient of two terms with equal powers |

narration.2: A placeholder node in front of the result, so appending never needs a special case for the first term.
narration.3: tail always points at the last node of the result built so far.
narration.7: Merge while both polynomials still have terms.
narration.8: The front of poly1 has the higher power, so it comes next in the sum.
narration.9: Link that node after the result's tail.
narration.11: Move on to poly1's next term.
narration.12: The front of poly2 has the higher power, so it comes next.
narration.15: Move on to poly2's next term.
narration.17: Equal powers: their coefficients add up.
narration.18: Only a non-zero total becomes a term; cancelled terms disappear.
narration.19: Append a new node holding the combined term.
narration.22: Both terms are used up, so advance both lists.
narration.26: Whatever remains in the unfinished list has lower powers; attach it as is.
narration.27: Skip the placeholder; this is null when every term cancelled.
